options.a: Default risk reflected in a bond's credit spread
options.b: Time remaining until a bond matures
options.c: A stock's sensitivity to the market
options.d: Bond price sensitivity to rate changes

distractorExplanations.a: Credit spread and default risk measure issuer quality; duration measures price sensitivity to interest-rate changes.
distractorExplanations.b: Maturity is a date; duration weights the timing of all cash flows.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensitivity of a stock to the market is beta.

options.a: A foreign ordinary share listed on its home-country exchange
options.b: A U.S. company's shares sold to foreign buyers
options.c: A fund that holds a basket of foreign stocks
options.d: A U.S.-traded receipt for foreign company shares

distractorExplanations.a: That describes the underlying ordinary share; the ADR is a U.S.-traded receipt issued by a depositary bank against it.
distractorExplanations.b: ADRs represent foreign issuers' shares, not U.S. companies'.
distractorExplanations.c: A basket of foreign stocks is a fund, while an ADR represents one issuer.

options.a: Mortgage loans insured by federal agencies
options.b: Real estate cash flows via a pooled security
options.c: Direct ownership of a single rental property
options.d: Construction loans made to homebuilders

distractorExplanations.a: Agency-insured mortgages describe GNMA pass-throughs, not REITs.
distractorExplanations.c: REIT holders own shares in a portfolio, not title to a property.
distractorExplanations.d: Some mortgage REITs lend, but REITs mainly give pooled real estate exposure.

options.a: Gets dividend priority over common, with limited votes
options.b: Has voting rights but is paid after common holders
options.c: Pays variable dividends that rise with earnings
options.d: Ranks ahead of bondholders when a corporation is liquidated

distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the liquidation order: bondholders and other creditors are paid before preferred stockholders.
distractorExplanations.b: Preferred holders are paid before common and usually cannot vote.
distractorExplanations.c: Preferred dividends are usually fixed; common dividends vary with earnings.

options.a: Buys more of the best performers to add momentum
options.b: Changes target weights to follow market trends
options.c: Moves the full portfolio to cash after losses
options.d: Sells winners and buys laggards to reset targets

distractorExplanations.a: Adding to winners increases drift from targets, the opposite of rebalancing.
distractorExplanations.b: Rebalancing restores existing targets; it does not chase trends.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving to cash after losses is market timing, not rebalancing.

options.a: Put the client's interests ahead of its own
options.b: Recommend only products that are suitable
options.c: Disclose conflicts when the client asks about them
options.d: Choose the lowest-cost product for each client

distractorExplanations.c: Fiduciaries must proactively disclose material conflicts; waiting for the client to ask does not satisfy the duty of loyalty.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty of care weighs cost among many factors; it does not require picking the cheapest product for every client.
distractorExplanations.b: Suitability is a lower standard than the fiduciary duty of loyalty.

options.a: Specific securities to buy each quarter
options.b: Goals, constraints, risk, and allocation
options.c: A projected return target for each year
options.d: The adviser's fee schedule and billing method

distractorExplanations.d: Fees and billing belong in the advisory contract and Form ADV Part 2A; the IPS sets objectives, constraints, and allocation.
distractorExplanations.a: An IPS sets policy and ranges, not a list of trades.
distractorExplanations.c: An IPS may state a required return, but not a promised annual target.

options.a: Investing a lump sum when prices look low
options.b: Buying the same number of shares at regular intervals
options.c: Investing a fixed dollar amount at intervals
options.d: Selling a fixed dollar amount each month

distractorExplanations.b: A fixed share count is not DCA; DCA invests a fixed dollar amount, so more shares are bought when prices are low.
distractorExplanations.a: Buying on perceived lows is market timing.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed withdrawals are a systematic withdrawal plan.

options.a: Reduce unsystematic risk through low correlation
options.b: Eliminate systematic market risk by holding many securities
options.c: Raise expected return without adding risk
options.d: Replace the need to set an asset allocation

distractorExplanations.b: Diversification cannot remove systematic (market) risk; it reduces only unsystematic, company-specific risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Diversification improves risk-adjusted return but does not raise return for free.
distractorExplanations.d: Diversification works within an allocation; it does not replace one.

options.a: The client's age as the single deciding factor
options.b: The client's past returns in other accounts
options.c: The risk level of the firm's recommended model portfolio
options.d: Willingness and ability to take risk, plus goals

distractorExplanations.c: Risk tolerance is a client attribute; the firm's model portfolio is chosen after assessing it, not used to define it.
distractorExplanations.a: Age matters, but it is only one input.
distractorExplanations.b: Past returns do not show willingness or capacity to bear losses.

options.a: Everyone pays the same percentage of income
options.b: Tax rates fall as taxable income rises
options.c: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises
options.d: Taxes are based on spending, not income

distractorExplanations.a: One rate for all income levels is a flat tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Falling rates as income rises is a regressive system.
distractorExplanations.d: Taxes on spending are consumption taxes, such as sales taxes.

options.a: Published analyst research reports sent to clients
options.b: Public information that is not yet widely known
options.c: Material nonpublic information in breach of duty
options.d: Rumors discussed on public investment forums

distractorExplanations.a: Research that has been published and distributed to clients is public information, so trading on it is not insider trading.
distractorExplanations.b: Public information, even if obscure, is not insider information.
distractorExplanations.d: Public rumors are not material nonpublic information from an insider.

options.a: The lowest commission rate, even if execution quality suffers
options.b: Execution through the adviser's affiliated broker
options.c: The fastest available venue, even at a worse fill price
options.d: The most favorable overall execution reasonably available

distractorExplanations.a: Best execution weighs price, speed, likelihood of execution, and service; the lowest commission alone does not satisfy it.
distractorExplanations.c: Speed is only one factor; a fast fill at an inferior price can violate the duty to seek the most favorable overall terms.
distractorExplanations.b: An affiliated broker may be used only if it delivers best execution.

options.a: Verbal consent after the trade has settled
options.b: Approval from the firm's compliance officer
options.c: Disclosure in the client's year-end account statement
options.d: Written disclosure and consent before settlement

distractorExplanations.c: After-the-fact disclosure in a statement is too late; Advisers Act Section 206(3) requires written disclosure and consent before completion.
distractorExplanations.a: Consent must be obtained before completion of the trade and in writing.
distractorExplanations.b: Internal approval does not replace client consent.

options.a: The value of the next-best alternative forgone
options.b: The total out-of-pocket cost paid to carry out a decision
options.c: The sunk cost of a past investment decision
options.d: The extra return earned over a benchmark

distractorExplanations.b: Out-of-pocket cost is the explicit cost; opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up.
distractorExplanations.c: Sunk costs are already spent and should not affect decisions.
distractorExplanations.d: Return above a benchmark is alpha.

options.a: Lower than short-term yields
options.b: Higher than short-term yields
options.c: Equal to short-term yields
options.d: Set directly by the Federal Reserve

distractorExplanations.d: The Fed targets the short-term federal funds rate; long-term Treasury yields are set by market supply and demand.
distractorExplanations.a: Long yields below short yields describe an inverted curve.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal yields across maturities describe a flat curve.

options.a: Open-market operations
options.b: Changes to the discount rate
options.c: Government spending and taxation
options.d: Changes to bank reserve requirements

distractorExplanations.d: Reserve requirements are a Federal Reserve monetary policy tool; fiscal policy is government spending and taxation.
distractorExplanations.a: Open-market operations are monetary policy run by the Fed.
distractorExplanations.b: The discount rate is a Federal Reserve tool.

options.a: Raises the company's total market value
options.b: Lowers share count and raises share price
options.c: Dilutes each holder's percentage ownership in the company
options.d: Raises share count, lowers price, same value

distractorExplanations.c: A split gives every holder proportionally more shares, so each holder's percentage ownership stays the same.
distractorExplanations.a: A split does not change the company's total value.
distractorExplanations.b: Fewer shares at a higher price describe a reverse split.

options.a: Issued by the company, often with long terms
options.b: Standardized contracts cleared by the OCC
options.c: Created by investors writing contracts
options.d: Rights to sell the issuer's stock at a set price

distractorExplanations.d: A right to sell at a set price is a put; warrants are long-term rights to buy stock from the issuing company.
distractorExplanations.b: OCC-cleared standardized contracts are listed options.
distractorExplanations.c: Options are written by investors; warrants come from the issuer.

options.a: The credit rating of the mortgage servicer
options.b: The coupon rate on the underlying mortgages
options.c: Prepayment speed and the tranche's priority
options.d: The number of tranches in the CMO structure

distractorExplanations.a: Servicer ratings matter little to tranche risk.
distractorExplanations.b: The coupon matters less than how prepayments are allocated.
distractorExplanations.d: Tranche count alone does not define a tranche's risk.

options.a: Buy-and-hold investors unfamiliar with compounding
options.b: Day traders who monitor and close positions each day
options.c: Traders using it briefly with a clear strategy
options.d: Institutions hedging short-term index exposure

distractorExplanations.b: Leveraged ETFs are designed for one-day horizons, so actively monitored day trading is the use they are built for.
distractorExplanations.c: Short-term tactical use with understanding fits the design.
distractorExplanations.d: Short-term institutional hedging matches the daily reset.

options.a: Market risk on the protected principal
options.b: Issuer credit risk if the bank defaults
options.c: Daily repricing of the principal amount
options.d: SIPC limits on the principal guarantee

distractorExplanations.a: Principal is protected at maturity if the issuer pays.
distractorExplanations.c: Protected principal is set at maturity, not repriced daily.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC does not guarantee structured note principal.

options.a: Liquidity, stable income, and preservation
options.b: Growth stocks for long-term capital appreciation
options.c: Long-dated zero-coupon bonds for yield
options.d: Emerging market funds for diversification

distractorExplanations.b: Growth stocks pay little income and are volatile, which conflicts with a conservative retiree's need for income and preservation.
distractorExplanations.c: Zeros pay no current income and are volatile.
distractorExplanations.d: Emerging markets add risk and are not income-focused.

options.a: Whether the IRA offers more fund choices
options.b: Taxes, fees, investment options, services
options.c: Whether the plan allows in-service loans
options.d: The client's age compared with retirement

distractorExplanations.a: More choices is one factor, not the full comparison.
distractorExplanations.c: Loan access is one plan feature among many.
distractorExplanations.d: Age matters, but the comparison covers costs, options, and services.

options.a: Document each profile and plan for joint goals
options.b: Use the more aggressive spouse's tolerance
options.c: Use the more conservative spouse's tolerance for all assets
options.d: Average both risk scores into one profile

distractorExplanations.c: Defaulting to one spouse's profile ignores the other's goals; each profile should be documented and reconciled for joint goals.
distractorExplanations.b: Ignoring one spouse's comfort risks unsuitable recommendations.
distractorExplanations.d: Averaging hides real differences that should be discussed.

options.a: Their prices do not change with interest rates
options.b: Interest may be exempt from federal income tax
options.c: They pay higher yields than corporate bonds
options.d: They are backed by the full faith of the U.S. Treasury

distractorExplanations.d: Municipal bonds are backed by state or local issuers' taxing power or project revenue, not by the U.S. Treasury.
distractorExplanations.a: Muni bond funds lose value when rates rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Munis usually pay lower nominal yields than corporates.

options.a: Allowed if the new annuity has lower fees
options.b: Allowed if the client signs a disclosure form
options.c: Allowed if the old contract is past surrender
options.d: Avoided unless a documented net benefit exists

distractorExplanations.a: Lower fees alone may not offset surrender charges or lost benefits.
distractorExplanations.b: A signature does not make an unsuitable exchange suitable.
distractorExplanations.c: Even past surrender, lost benefits must be weighed.

options.a: Interest costs, maintenance calls, magnified losses
options.b: The firm's margin rate compared with competitors
options.c: Tax deductions available for the margin interest paid
options.d: Historical returns of margin-financed accounts

distractorExplanations.c: Interest deductibility is a tax planning point; the required margin disclosures are interest cost, maintenance calls, and amplified losses.
distractorExplanations.b: Rate comparisons are not the required risk disclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: Past returns do not disclose margin risks.

options.a: Filling client orders ahead of firm orders
options.b: Combining client orders into one block trade
options.c: Delaying a client order to seek a better fill for the client
options.d: Trading ahead of client orders for personal gain

distractorExplanations.c: Working an order for the client's benefit is order handling, not front-running, which is trading ahead for personal gain.
distractorExplanations.a: Putting clients first is the correct priority, not front-running.
distractorExplanations.b: Block trading is legitimate when allocations are fair.

options.a: Illegal tipping under insider trading rules
options.b: Allowed if the friends do not trade on it
options.c: Allowed if no payment is received for it
options.d: Allowed if shared after market hours

distractorExplanations.b: Tipping itself can violate the law, and liability arises if friends trade.
distractorExplanations.c: A personal benefit can be non-monetary, such as a gift to a friend.
distractorExplanations.d: Timing does not change the nonpublic nature of the information.

options.a: Disclosure to the client but no firm approval
options.b: Return of the gift within one year
options.c: Supervisory approval and firm policy compliance
options.d: Reporting to the state administrator within 30 days

distractorExplanations.d: Gifts are governed by firm policy and supervisory review; there is no 30-day gift report to the state administrator.
distractorExplanations.a: Firm policy and supervision govern gifts, not only client disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Firms apply limits and approval, not a one-year return rule.

options.a: Written notice to the firm and its approval
options.b: Verbal notice to the branch manager before the sale
options.c: Client consent without telling the firm
options.d: Disclosure on the next annual U4 update

distractorExplanations.b: FINRA Rule 3280 requires prior written notice to the member firm, and written approval when the person is compensated.
distractorExplanations.c: Client consent does not replace firm notice and approval.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure must come before the transaction, not afterward.

options.a: Present projected values as contractual values
options.b: Use the highest rate the insurer allows
options.c: Disclose assumptions and non-guarantees
options.d: Leave out fees to keep the page simple

distractorExplanations.a: Illustrations show projections based on assumed rates; presenting them as contractual values misrepresents non-guaranteed elements.
distractorExplanations.b: Using the top rate without labeling it misleads clients.
distractorExplanations.d: Omitting fees overstates results.

options.a: Violates confidentiality and firm policy
options.b: Is allowed if the complaint was resolved
options.c: Is allowed if the name is partly hidden
options.d: Is allowed if the client posted it first

distractorExplanations.b: Resolution does not permit public disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: Partial redaction can still identify the client.
distractorExplanations.d: A client's post does not waive the firm's confidentiality duty.

options.a: Required disclosure on the firm's website
options.b: Pay-to-play restrictions with governments
options.c: Automatic registration as a lobbyist
options.d: Limits on the firm's advertising budget

distractorExplanations.a: The issue is business restrictions, not web disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: Contributions do not trigger lobbyist registration under securities rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Pay-to-play rules restrict government business, not ad budgets.

options.a: Wait to see if the market moves in its favor
options.b: Charge the loss to the client with a notice
options.c: Split the loss between client and firm
options.d: Correct it, document it, use error procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting on the market is speculation with the client's money.
distractorExplanations.b: Clients should not bear losses from firm errors.
distractorExplanations.c: The firm bears its own errors; splitting shifts cost to the client.

options.a: Personal trades ahead of pending client orders
options.b: Pre-clearing personal trades with compliance
options.c: Allocating IPO shares under a written, fair allocation policy
options.d: Disclosing soft-dollar use in Form ADV

distractorExplanations.c: Allocating IPO shares by a written, fair policy is expected practice; it prevents favoritism rather than being prohibited.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-clearance is a required control, not a violation.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosing soft dollars is required.

options.a: Public offerings of new issuer securities
options.b: Isolated non-issuer trades between investors
options.c: Sales by agents who are not registered in the state
options.d: Offers made through public advertising

distractorExplanations.c: Exempt transactions excuse the security from registration; they do not let unregistered agents sell in the state.
distractorExplanations.a: Public issuer offerings generally require registration.
distractorExplanations.d: Public advertising usually defeats private exemptions.

options.a: Is covered by FINRA membership instead
options.b: May register with the state afterward
options.c: May face state penalties and injunctions
options.d: Is exempt if it has no local office

distractorExplanations.a: FINRA membership does not replace state registration.
distractorExplanations.b: Late registration does not cure past violations.
distractorExplanations.d: Soliciting residents without an office can still require registration.

options.a: Replace state laws with one federal statute
options.b: Set uniform commission rates for broker-dealers
options.c: Approve all securities offered to investors
options.d: Harmonize exam content and registration rules

distractorExplanations.b: Neither NASAA nor the states set commission rates; compensation is subject only to fairness and disclosure rules.
distractorExplanations.a: NASAA coordinates states; it does not replace state law.
distractorExplanations.c: Many offerings are federal covered and exempt from state review.
